target.thesis: Austin's A/B conditions make no demand for intention to perform an act, and sincerity-grade states fall under Γ (abuse). Intention-based denials therefore import a non-Austinian condition and owe an argument that apology, promise and similar act types are intention-constituted rather than procedure-constituted. For proxy-occupied roles the question is one of status; for an LLM acting in its own name it may reduce to standing that tracks mind-involving capacities.
target.headline: The intention-based denials of LLM speech acts mistake what Austin classed as an abuse (a hollow but performed act) for a misfire (an unperformed act), so the live question is whether LLM output meets Austin's A/B procedural conditions, which is a question about status and not about mind.
target.target: Gubelmann, Magnus/Buccella/D'Cruz, and the shared assumption (including Attah's) that communicative intention is a performance condition for speech acts
target.sketch: Austin separates misfires, where the act is void because there is no accepted procedure, the wrong persons or circumstances, or a flawed execution, from abuses, where the act is performed but insincere because the speaker lacks the requisite thoughts, feelings or intentions (the Γ conditions). Gubelmann, Magnus et al., and the Gricean-intention framing all argue that missing intentions, remorse or agency means no act is performed. On Austin's own taxonomy that shows at most a defective apology, promise or assertion. A bare lack of sincerity-grade states is also what Searle treats as compatible with performing an insincere assertion. The intention requirement only becomes a performance condition after the Strawsonian/Gricean rewrite of Austin, and the debate has silently adopted that rewrite. If Austin is restored, the question becomes whether a given LLM output occupies a role in a conventional procedure, which is the Butlin–Viebahn and Skiba normative-status question. The positions then regroup: the organismic denials become claims about abuse, the proxy views become claims about who occupies the A-condition role, and the decisive disagreement shifts to which act types are conventional-procedural and which are intention-constituted. The key premise is that the speech-act kinds in question (apology, promise, advice) are at least partly procedure-constituted.

findings.part: Mapping the LLM case onto Austin's Γ/abuse category (lack of sincerity-grade states = at most a defective act)
findings.source: Anonymous ("Ryle and Jack"), "How Chatbots Do Things With Words", Substack essay, c. 2026
findings.what_they_say: The essay applies Austin's misfire/abuse scheme to chatbots. <cite index="60-1">It says abuse involves insincerity, but chatbots lack the capacity for sincerity or insincerity because they lack intention.</cite> <cite index="60-4">It concludes that Austin's abuse category does not capture what chatbots do when they generate an apology.</cite>
findings.note: This is the closest antecedent for applying Austin's misfire/abuse taxonomy to chatbots. It argues the opposite on the Γ mapping, so it is a rival to answer. It is a non-peer-reviewed blog essay seen only as a snippet, so it is not an anticipation.

findings.part: Claim that Austin's taxonomy makes no demand for intention to perform an act
findings.source: Kevin Halion, "Deconstruction and Speech Act Theory" (web thesis); Witczak-Plisiecka, "From Speech Acts to Speech Actions"
findings.what_they_say: Halion reports Austin saying that performatives are subject to dimensions of unsatisfactoriness common to all actions, distinct from the infelicities. <cite index="30-19">He cites HDTW p. 21 for this.</cite> Witczak-Plisiecka's snippet reads <cite index="7-1">performance as discussed by Austin is always intentional</cite>.
findings.note: A referee can say Austin presupposes agency or intention in the general theory of action, outside A/B/Γ. This is a rival reading that the thesis must address. It is not a foreclosure.

findings.part: Named target: Gubelmann holds that intention is a performance condition for speech acts
findings.source: Reto Gubelmann, "Large Language Models, Agency, and Why Speech Acts are Beyond Them (For Now)", Philosophy & Technology 37, 2024
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="4-7,4-8">Using language means acting, and LLMs cannot act because they lack intentions.</cite> <cite index="4-9">He grounds this in agents with intentions needing to be autonomous organisms, whereas LLMs are heteronomous mechanisms.</cite> A snippet of the full-text PDF has him argue that <cite index="2-4">speaking is a kind of action, and actions require intentions</cite>.
findings.note: The target holds the ascribed view. His argument is action-theoretic and general, not Austin-exegetical, so the thesis must answer an argument and not only an omission. I did not see him discuss Γ.

findings.part: Named target: Magnus/Buccella/D'Cruz hold that missing intention, remorse or agency means no apology is performed
findings.source: P.D. Magnus, A. Buccella, J. D'Cruz, "Chatbot apologies: beyond bullshit", AI and Ethics 5, 2025
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="56-14">They say apology is a speech act which requires an agent with certain capacities, and that chatbots lack those capacities.</cite> <cite index="56-12">They also say chatbots cannot offer more than rote apologies.</cite>
findings.note: The target holds a capacity-based denial, with moral and linguistic agency doing the work, so it is a rival. The 'rote apology' concession is compatible with a defective-act reading. The footnote calling apology a specimen performative (<cite index="10-11">Austin treats it as one</cite>) suggests they engage Austin. I saw no sign they use the misfire/abuse split.

findings.part: Named target: Attah is placed in the shared-assumption camp
findings.source: Nuhu Osman Attah, "Do language models lack communicative intentions?", Synthese, 2025 (also in Talking Machines)
findings.what_they_say: He targets the 'Communicative Intention argument', which he says is <cite index="27-5">driven by strong Gricean assumptions about linguistic competence that he argues are empirically untenable.</cite> <cite index="27-6">He finds no good reason to suppose LLMs lack communicative intentions.</cite> Williams describes Attah's interest as <cite index="19-11">the requirements for linguistic competence</cite>.
findings.note: Attah argues that LLMs may have communicative intentions and that the Gricean competence requirement is shaky. He does not, in what I saw, argue that intention is a performance condition on speech acts. The ascription to him should be reworded, since he is an opponent of the denial. Only the abstract was seen.

findings.part: The assumption that intention is a condition on speech acts is widespread and often unargued
findings.source: Iwan Williams, "Intention-like representations in language models?", Philosophical Studies, 2026; Williams & Bayne (?), "Chatting with Bots: AI, Speech Acts, and the Edge of Assertion" (arXiv 2410.16645; authors not shown in the snippet)
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="20-1">Capacities such as assertion are widely held to require intentions of one kind or another.</cite> The arXiv paper lists an 'attitudes objection', <cite index="50-11">that chatbots lack the capacity to form intentions, which gives reason to deny that their outputs are genuine acts.</cite>
findings.note: These are survey-style statements that the assumption is shared. They are evidence for the thesis's diagnosis, not a rival.

findings.part: Austin's Γ conditions: missing thoughts, feelings or intentions yield abuse, not failure of the act
findings.source: Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy, "Austin, John Langshaw"; Antony Eagle lecture notes quoting Austin 1956
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="31-1">The speaker's intentions play only a minor role in performing a speech act, and violating condition C.1 gives an abuse, not a failure of the speech act.</cite> Eagle quotes Austin: <cite index="33-13">using the formulae without the requisite thoughts, feelings or intentions is an abuse of the procedure, which is insincerity.</cite>
findings.note: Reference-work and lecture-note statements of the exegetical premise. They support the Austin reading and are not a rival.

findings.part: The intention requirement enters via the Strawson/Grice rewrite; the real dispute is which act types are conventional and which intention-constituted
findings.source: P.F. Strawson, "Intention and Convention in Speech Acts", Philosophical Review, 1964; Bach & Harnish via Sadock, "Speech Acts"; "Illocution, Perillocution and Communication", Palgrave
findings.what_they_say: A snippet of Strawson's text reads <cite index="65-15">some illocutionary acts are conventional; others are not.</cite> Sadock reports that Bach and Harnish <cite index="68-5">follow Strawson in distinguishing ceremonial acts, where convention is primary, from communicative acts like asking and stating, where intention is assumed.</cite> A Palgrave abstract says the conventionalist–intentionalist debate <cite index="69-4">goes back to Strawson's 1964 paper.</cite>
findings.note: This is the historical source of the dispute the thesis says the LLM debate has silently inherited. The conventionalist/intentionalist split by act type is already the decisive axis, so the thesis must credit it. It is also a rival on the key premise for non-ceremonial acts. Nothing seen applies the split to LLMs, and I did not check where apology or promise falls.

findings.part: Reframing the question as normative status/standing, and 'standing that tracks mind-involving capacities'
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="39-3">To be capable of assertion an entity must produce outputs with descriptive functions and be capable of being sanctioned by agents it interacts with.</cite> <cite index="39-6">They also consider AI systems generating proxy assertions on behalf of human agents.</cite> A citing paper reads them as holding that <cite index="38-7">LLMs lack intentions, understanding, interests and desires, and so are unsanctionable.</cite>
findings.note: PRECEDENT-or-ANTICIPATED is undecided for the final conjunct. They develop a sanctionability requirement for assertion at length, but I saw nothing on other act types or on Austin's taxonomy. The thesis's conjunct is hedged ('may reduce to'). The thesis already cites them.

findings.part: Norm-based rather than intention-based denial; generalisation to all speech acts
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="17-4">He shows how a norm-based argument against LLM-assertion can be generalised to support a negative answer on speech acts.</cite> A secondary summary says <cite index="46-5">this becomes a wholesale denial that LLMs perform speech acts of any kind.</cite>
findings.note: Skiba's route to denial is through constitutive norms and status, not intention. This is evidence that the debate already has a status-based line the thesis can build on or answer. It is a rival conclusion on the status question.

findings.part: Proxy views as claims about who occupies the A-condition role
findings.source: Green & Michel account as reported in "Against speech liberalism for generative AI" (2026); "Chatbots and Speech Act Responsibility Gaps", OUP chapter (author not shown in the snippet)
findings.what_they_say: On Green and Michel's account, <cite index="40-5">an artificial system may itself perform a speech act while acting on behalf of a person or institution whose commitments provide the normative basis.</cite> The OUP chapter says <cite index="47-9">the nature of speech acts metaphysically depends on accountability ascriptions.</cite>
findings.note: These are the proxy views the thesis wants to re-describe. They are normative-status accounts without an explicit Austinian A/Γ framing, in what I saw. I did not read the primary texts.

findings.part: Intention is not required for some illocutionary acts
findings.source: "Communicative Action in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Theorizing LLMs as Communicative and Strategic Agents", Philosophy & Technology, 2026
findings.what_they_say: They concede that an LLM <cite index="21-3">cannot perform intentional illocutionary speech acts.</cite> They add <cite index="21-7">a new category of behavioral speech acts that produce speech-act effects in lieu of psychological intentions.</cite>
findings.note: They deny that intention is needed for performing something speech-act-like, but by positing a new category and not through Austin's taxonomy. They concede the Gricean premise for standard acts, so they are not an anticipation.

findings.part: Shared assumption in the follow-on literature
findings.source: "Speech Acts and Large Language Models" (PhilArchive preprint; author not shown), ~2025
findings.what_they_say: The paper says chatbots <cite index="1-5">lack the intention required for genuine illocutionary acts.</cite> It adopts Gubelmann's view of intention as goal-orientation. It also calls chatbot speech acts <cite index="12-12">imperfect and yet effective.</cite>
findings.note: This shows Gubelmann's premise being taken over without argument. It is evidence for the diagnosis, not a rival.

findings.part: Adjacent empirical evidence: users classify chatbot apologies as insincere, not as non-apologies
findings.source: "A natural apology is sincere: Understanding chatbots' performance in symbolic recovery", ScienceDirect (service-recovery research); Ashktorab et al., "Who's Sorry Now", ACM
findings.what_they_say: <cite index="63-2">Chatbots' apology is viewed as unnatural and insincere by most customers.</cite> The ACM paper studies <cite index="11-2">user reactions to chatbot apologies as a means of recovering from errors.</cite>
findings.note: The sources are consumer/HCI research, not a psychology or linguistics study of apology constitution. The lay categorisation as 'insincere' fits the abuse reading, but this is weak evidence.

finding.what_is_left: Austin's taxonomy puts sincerity-grade states under Γ, so a denial that an LLM output is an apology or promise because it lacks intention or remorse needs a further premise that those act types are intention-constituted. The LLM literature I could see supplies intention-based (Gubelmann, Magnus et al.) or norm-based (Butlin–Viebahn, Skiba) premises, and none of the snippets or abstracts engages Γ directly. The thesis still has to answer three things: the reading on which Austin presupposes agency outside the infelicity taxonomy, the point that a system with no capacity for sincerity cannot be 'insincere', and the Strawson/Bach–Harnish view that non-ceremonial acts are intention-constituted. No work seen anticipated the thesis, but I could read the full text of none of them, so that is a statement about what I saw and not about the whole literature.
credit: Anonymous ("Ryle and Jack") 2026 — applying Austin's misfire/abuse scheme to chatbots, and the objection that lacking intention is not insincerity
Strawson 1964 and Bach & Harnish (via Sadock) — the conventional vs intention-constituted split by act type that the thesis says decides the matter
Butlin & Viebahn 2025 — normative status via sanctionability, and proxy assertion
Skiba 2026 — a norm-based generalised denial that does not rest on intention
Green & Michel (via the 2026 Phil. & Tech. paper) — an artificial system performing an act on behalf of a principal
Magnus, Buccella & D'Cruz 2025 — the 'rote apology' concession and the engagement with apology as a performative
Attah 2025 — a challenge to the Gricean communicative-intention premise in the LLM debate
finding.not_found: I found no peer-reviewed work applying Austin's A/B/Γ taxonomy to LLM speech acts, and no work arguing that intention-based denials import a non-Austinian condition. I saw only snippets or abstracts of the named targets, so I cannot say whether Gubelmann or Magnus et al. discuss Γ or misfire/abuse in full text. I did not search Searle on insincere assertion, so the Searle claim in the thesis is unverified here. I did not consult Austin's primary text, only secondary quotations. I did not find, or search specifically for, work on whether apology, promise or advice are conventional-procedural or intention-constituted (Searle, Alston, Bach–Harnish on apology, Austin on 'I apologize'). The empirical search stayed within HCI and consumer research. I did not search the psychology or linguistics of apology, promising or speech-act uptake, so the empirical check on this thesis is weak and should not be read as clean. I did not check Löhr 2026 or Williams & Bayne 2024 beyond citations by others, and I did not check the OUP chapter's authorship.

sep.why: The theses reread Austin's misfire/abuse taxonomy against intention-based denials that LLMs perform speech acts, so the speech-acts debate and the Austin entry are the core, with assertion covering the insincere-assertion and Searle/Gricean framing.

findings.position: Austin treats sincerity failure as an 'abuse', not a 'misfire'. The act is still performed but is infelicitous, so sincerity-grade states fall outside the conditions for the act's existence.
findings.who: Austin, as reported by the entry (Green)
findings.quote: Here I have promised all right, but the act is not felicitous because it is not sincere. My act is, more precisely, an abuse because although it is a speech act, it fails to live up to a standard appropriate for speech acts of its kind.
findings.note: Directly backs the claim that sincerity-grade states fall under the abuse class (Γ). The entry never uses the A/B/Γ labels.

findings.position: Austin's felicity conditions are procedural. An accepted conventional procedure, executed by the right persons in the right circumstances, is what makes the act. Searle follows in a weaker form, allowing some acts without constitutive rules.
findings.quote: There must exist an accepted conventional procedure having a certain conventional effect, that procedure to include the uttering of certain words by certain persons in certain circumstances…
findings.note: The entry quotes no Austinian condition requiring an intention to perform. This supports the thesis's reading of the A/B conditions, though the entry does not make that reading explicit.

findings.position: For status-bound acts, what matters is social standing or authority and uptake, not the speaker's mental state. Strawson's intentionalism itself concedes that conventions suffice for appointing and excommunicating.
findings.who: Austin; Searle and Vanderveken (preparatory conditions); Strawson (concession)
findings.quote: a person cannot marry a couple unless she is legally invested with the authority to do so.
findings.note: Gives the thesis a footing for its 'proxy-occupied roles are a question of status' point. The entry says nothing about proxies.

findings.position: The entry's own account defines speech acts through speaker meaning and overt commitment. It argues that conventions cannot substitute for the intention to put a sentence forth as an assertion. It says it is hard to see how one could perform a speech act with no intention of performing a speech act at all. This is a rival intention-based account, but it does not conclusively close off the thesis.
findings.who: Strawson 1964; Green (entry author, 1997, 2013); Grice-style speaker meaning
findings.quote: Just as no convention could make it the case that I believe that P, so too no convention could make it the case that I intend to put forth a certain sentence as an assertion.
findings.note: This is the position the thesis says 'owes an argument'. The entry's author holds that intention is required for non-conventional acts, and the thesis must answer that.

findings.position: The somniloquist case, the point that speech acts need speaker meaning, and the 'trying to ask' cases show that the words plus a procedure are not always enough. The speaker must also intentionally undertake a publicly accessible commitment.
findings.quote: speech acts involve intentional undertaking of a publicly accessible commitment
findings.note: A referee will use this to argue that procedure alone does not suffice, even for acts that look procedure-constituted.

findings.position: A society could have a convention that uttering certain expressions constitutes an illocutionary act, even on stage or in jokes. This is a procedure-constitutes-act position. Green replies that it does not work for assertion, which needs intentions.
findings.quote: there could be a society with a convention that utterance of a certain expression constituted performance of a certain illocutionary act
findings.note: This is the nearest the entry comes to procedure-constituted force with no intention required. It is explored briefly and then limited.

findings.position: Speaker meaning need not involve intentions to affect an addressee (infants, photocopiers, photos). Speaker meaning is instead construed as overtly manifesting one's commitments or state of mind. This bears on whether mind-involving capacities are what matter for non-human speakers.
findings.quote: Davis (1992) provides a range of cases such as speaking to pre-linguistic infants, uncooperative photocopy machines, and photos of deceased loved ones.
findings.note: Relevant to the 'standing that tracks mind-involving capacities' clause. The entry does not take up artificial speakers.

nearest_positions: Force conventionalism: acts are constituted by conventional procedure and constitutive rules, with sincerity as a separate matter of abuse — Austin (strong), Searle (weaker)
Intentionalism: acts are explained by manifest communicative intentions, with conventions only for special institutional cases — Strawson 1964, with Grice-style speaker meaning

Green's overt-commitment account: a speech act is performed by overtly undertaking a norm-governed commitment, either by invoking a convention or by manifesting an intention — Green (the entry's author)
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: LLMs and other artificial speakers, proxy-occupied roles, and any 'standing' that tracks mind-involving capacities. It also never labels Austin's conditions A/B/Γ and never says that Austin's conditions omit an intention-to-perform requirement. It does not frame intention-based denials of apology or promise as importing a non-Austinian condition.

findings.position: The entry reports Austin's two kinds of infelicity. Misfires are failures of procedure, persons or circumstances, in which the act is not achieved. Abuses are insincere performances in which the act is performed. This matches the thesis's split between A/B conditions and Γ (sincerity-grade states).
findings.who: Austin 1962b, as reported by the entry
findings.quote: Second, there are abuses: in these cases, the act is performed, but insincerely, perhaps for example in instituting a marriage of convenience.
findings.note: The entry gives the thesis its textual base. The A/B/Γ labels and the claim that the A/B conditions have no intention requirement are not in the entry.

findings.position: The entry's examples of misfires are all procedural or status failures (wrong formula, already married, wrong officiant), not failures of intention. This fits the 'procedure-constituted' reading of act types.
findings.who: Austin 1962b: 15–16, as reported by the entry
findings.quote: …if we…utter the formula incorrectly, or if…we are not in a position to do the act because we are…married already, or it is the purser and not the captain who is conducting the ceremony, then the act in question, …marrying, is not successfully performed at all
findings.note: Supports the status/standing focus for proxy-occupied roles, but only by example.

findings.position: The entry credits Austin with a general challenge to simple sentence–act and sentence–truth pairings, and says the same sentence can perform several acts at once. A referee could use this against any rigid claim that an act type is constituted by one condition, whether procedure or intention.
findings.who: Austin, as reported by the entry
findings.quote: the possibility that we might sometimes do more than one thing in using a performative puts pressure on the idea that there is a simple connection between sentences and the various things we do in using them.
findings.note: Does not contradict the thesis. It is a point the thesis must handle when it says 'procedure-constituted' for particular act types.

findings.position: The entry lists intention-oriented speech-act theorists (Bach and Harnish, Searle, Schiffer, Strawson on illocutionary acts, Hornsby) only as references, with no description of their views. They are the likely source of the 'intention-based denials' the thesis targets.
findings.who: Bach and Harnish 1979; Searle 1968, 1969; Schiffer 1972; Strawson 1964a; Hornsby 1988
findings.quote: (For discussion of Austin’s distinction amongst locutionary, illocutionary, and perlocutionary acts see Bach 1975; Bach and Harnish 1979; … Searle 1968, 1969; Strawson 1964a, 1973; …)
findings.note: Bibliography only. The entry does not say they impose an intention condition, so who the thesis's rivals are has to be sourced elsewhere.

findings.position: The entry flags that Austin separates serious from non-serious uses of language, and that Derrida and Searle disputed the priority this gives. This is the closest the entry comes to discussing what makes an utterance count as a genuine act. The entry sets it aside.
findings.quote: Jacques Derrida challenged the standing of the distinction and the priority that Austin seemed to accord to some of what he counted as serious uses.
findings.note: The entry explicitly declines to discuss it.

nearest_positions: Austin's misfire/abuse distinction: misfires void the act, abuses (insincerity) leave it performed — Austin 1962b, as reported in the entry
Austin's rejection of a simple constative/performative sorting, with the illocutionary act as the primary object of assessment — Austin, as reported in the entry
Intention-oriented speech-act theory (Searle, Bach and Harnish, Schiffer, Strawson) — named only in the entry's bibliography, not described
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: Nearly everything specific to the thesis. The entry does not use the A/B/Γ labels or say that A/B impose no intention requirement. It does not discuss whether apologising or promising is intention-constituted or procedure-constituted, or any 'intention-based denial' of speech acts. It says nothing about proxy-occupied roles, LLMs or artificial agents acting in their own name, or standing that tracks mind-involving capacities.

findings.position: On Austin's own treatment, insincerity (the lacking state or intention) is an infelicity of the 'abuse' kind. It does not stop the act from being performed. The entry also lists flaw-type misexecutions and misinvocations as separate infelicity types.
findings.who: Austin (1962), as reported by the entry
findings.quote: an assertion is insincere in case of lying as a promise is insincere when the appropriate intention is lacking (Austin 1962 [1975: 40]). This is an infelicity of the abuse kind.
findings.note: Supplies the textual base for the thesis's claim that sincerity-grade states fall under abuse. The entry does not use the A/B/Γ labels or discuss them.

findings.position: Austin held that illocutionary acts are conventional, that is, they can be made explicit by the performative formula. On his view the act is performed once the procedure is invoked and uptake is secured, which is a procedure-constituted picture.
findings.quote: Austin held that illocutionary acts as opposed to perlocutionary acts are conventional, in the sense that they can be made explicit by the so-called performative formula
findings.note: The entry gives the procedure-constituted side the thesis relies on, and it reports defenders of that side.

findings.position: Austin's felicity conditions, and the idea that a failed presupposition makes an act void in the way a wrong legal formula does, are a broader view that the thesis applies to the intention-based denial question. The entry does not draw that application.
findings.who: Austin (1962), as reported by the entry
findings.quote: an infelicity of the same kind—flaw-type misexecutions—as the use of the wrong formula in a legal procedure
findings.note: The thesis applies Austin's framework. It is not pre-empted, because the entry never turns it against intention-based accounts.

findings.position: Rival, intention-based accounts treat illocutionary types as constituted by communicative or reflexive intentions, not by procedure. Strawson says convention plays little role for ordinary illocutionary types, and Stainton says convention is not necessary for assertion. Davidson and Bach & Harnish say convention is not sufficient.
findings.who: Strawson (1964); Searle (1969); Bach & Harnish (1979); Grice; Davidson; Stainton
findings.quote: If Strawson and Stainton are right, convention isn't necessary for making assertions.
findings.note: These are rivals the thesis must answer. None is reported as conclusively closing off a procedural view; Kölbel replies to Davidson, and García-Carpintero is cited as showing the constitutive-rule/convention question is controversial.

findings.position: The entry leaves open whether intention is needed at all for assertion. It also notes that Austin's uptake requirement is less plausible for speaker–content acts like asserting, since Bill can assert that p even though Lisa left the room.
findings.who: The entry's own question; Austin on uptake
findings.quote: must he intend it to be an assertion? Must it be made voluntarily?
findings.note: A referee would raise this. It shows the intention requirement is flagged as open, not settled.

findings.position: Commitment accounts treat assertion as a normative status taken on (accountability, liability to challenge). This is the nearest thing in the entry to the thesis's 'standing' and 'status'. They are not tied to proxies or to machines.
findings.quote: Making an assertion has normative consequences.
findings.note: A status-based route that the thesis's closing 'standing' proposal would need to be situated against.

nearest_positions: Communicative-intention analyses of illocutionary acts (reflexive intentions) — Grice, Strawson (1964), Searle (1969), Bach & Harnish (1979), with Sperber & Wilson's criticism

Convention-based accounts of illocutionary force versus the objections that convention is neither necessary nor sufficient — Austin, Dummett, Searle, Kölbel versus Strawson, Stainton, Davidson, Bach & Harnish
Commitment or status accounts of assertion — Peirce, Brandom, Alston, Green, Searle
per_thesis.entry_silent_on: The entry says nothing about LLMs or other artificial speakers, proxy-occupied roles, or 'standing' tied to mind-involving capacities. It does not discuss apology, and it never uses Austin's A/B/Γ labelling. It does not argue that denials of speech-act performance for lack of intention import a non-Austinian condition. It names only promising and asserting as acts whose constitution is disputed.

theses: Austin's A/B conditions make no demand for intention to perform an act, and sincerity-grade states fall under Γ (abuse). Intention-based denials therefore import a non-Austinian condition and owe an argument that apology, promise and similar act types are intention-constituted rather than procedure-constituted. For proxy-occupied roles the question is one of status; for an LLM acting in its own name it may reduce to standing that tracks mind-involving capacities.
